questions.q: Per this lesson, why can a technically excellent architecture still fail a review board evaluation?
options: Review boards grade what they were able to understand and probe in the time available, not the artifact in isolation -- a poorly presented design gives them nothing to evaluate
Technically excellent designs always pass regardless of presentation
Boards only evaluate the written documentation, never the live presentation
It is impossible for a correct design to ever fail a review
questions.explain: A board can only evaluate what it actually understood and got to probe during the session -- a design that lives entirely in the presenter's head or in dense unexplained slides doesn't give the board anything to engage with, regardless of how sound the underlying design is.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend identifying each kind of reviewer's likely concerns before presenting, rather than preparing one generic presentation?
options: Because every board member always asks about security specifically
Because a mixed-specialty panel each have different concerns, and a generic presentation risks quietly skipping the concern a specialist would go looking for first
Because boards are legally required to have exactly one specialist per domain
Because reviewers never ask questions outside their own specialty
questions.explain: A panel might include a security specialist, an integration specialist, and a generalist, each with different concerns -- the fix isn't a dedicated slide per specialty, but making sure the core narrative doesn't skip what a given specialist would look for first.

questions.q: What problem does opening a presentation with the business scenario and constraints, before any architecture diagram, specifically solve?
options: It has no real effect on how the board receives the technical content
It prevents reviewers from spending their early attention reverse-engineering the business context from technical choices, instead of evaluating the design
It is required by Salesforce's exam rules for every presentation
It eliminates the need to ever explain a design decision later
questions.explain: Reviewers who don't yet know the requirements will spend early minutes trying to infer business context from technical choices -- minutes that should instead go toward evaluating the design. Leading with the problem gives every later decision an already-understood justification.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why are diagrams described as carrying the architectural argument rather than prose?
options: Prose is always factually more accurate than a diagram
Systems are inherently relational, and a clear diagram shows those relationships directly instead of forcing the reader to mentally reconstruct them from a paragraph
Diagrams are only used when prose would be too long to fit on a slide
Boards are not permitted to ask questions about diagrams
questions.explain: Because systems are made of components connected to other components, a legible diagram shows that structure directly -- prose forces the reader to rebuild the same relationships mentally, which is slower and more error-prone during a live evaluation.

questions.q: Which of these is a recurring, avoidable presentation failure this lesson describes, distinct from the design itself being wrong?
options: Presenting every component at the same level of detail, so the board can't tell which decisions are actually load-bearing
Including a diagram at all
Mentioning the business problem before the architecture
Narrating a diagram out loud while showing it
questions.explain: Flattening every component to the same level of emphasis hides which two or three decisions actually matter most -- the other three options are recommended practices from this lesson, not failures.
